title: Telling Time in German: Quick Summary
items: **Halb acht is 7:30, not 8:30.** German hangs the half hour on the hour that is coming, so **halb acht** means half an hour before eight. This is the single mistake that costs visitors a table, a tour or a train.

**Written German time is a 24-hour clock.** Museum pages, shop doors, tickets and timetables use forms like **10:00 - 18:00 Uhr**, **bis 22 Uhr** and **20:15**. Spoken German drops back to twelve, which is where halb starts causing trouble.

**Viertel nach acht (8:15) and viertel vor neun (8:45) work everywhere.** Around Berlin and across eastern Germany you will also hear **viertel neun** for 8:15 and **dreiviertel neun** for 8:45, counting up towards nine instead of back from it.

**The two-letter day codes catch more people than the numbers.** Mo, Di, Mi, Do, Fr, Sa, So. **Di is Tuesday** and **Do is Thursday**. The Neues Museum on Museum Island reads **Mo geschlossen, Di 10:00 - 18:00 Uhr**, and most state museums keep the same Monday closure.

**Einlass is when you may go in, Beginn is when it starts, and letzter Einlass is the deadline that matters.** Last admission is usually **30 to 60 minutes before closing**, so bis 18 Uhr rarely means you can walk in at 17:55.
**My rule: say the time back as a number.** **Also 19:30?** Nobody minds the check, and it turns every halb, viertel and dreiviertel into something you cannot misread.
